titolo: Why Did Russia Unify as a Country But Europe Never Did?
descrizione:
One country covers 17 million square kilometers. The rest of Europe is about a third of that size and holds 43 countries. How did one side become a single giant while the other never came together? We follow the rivers, the Mongols, the fur trade and the armies that died on the plain.

From Ivan the Money Bag to Napoleon and Hitler, from the Peace of Westphalia to the European market, this is the story of how geography shaped power and money. Russia won the land. Europe won the money.

scene.testo: One country stretches across 17 million square kilometers. A Mongol bell, a sable fortune, and a burning Moscow. Why did one side become a giant?
Two men almost united Europe, and the same land destroyed both. And the winner ended up poorer. Why?

eventi.descrizione: French emperor, bicorne hat, grey coat

scene.testo: In 1648, a Russian sailor rounded the far eastern tip of Asia. His country already stretched from Europe to the Pacific.
That same year, Europe's rulers signed the Peace of Westphalia, often called the birth of a Europe of separate sovereign states.
Today, Russia is one country of 17 million square kilometers, nearly as big as the whole surface of Pluto.

eventi.testo: About the surface area of Pluto

scene.testo: The rest of Europe is about a third of that size, and it's split into 43 countries.
So why did one side become a single giant while the other never came together? And no, it's not just that Siberia was empty.

eventi.testo: Empty land is only part of it

scene.testo: The strange part is that the land that built Russia is the same land that destroyed the two men who came closest to uniting Europe.

eventi.testo: The same land destroyed two conquerors

scene.testo: And the side that won all that land? It ended up the poorer one.
Start with the ground. Russia was born on the East European Plain, about 4 million square kilometers of land.

eventi.testo: Russia was born on a plain

scene.testo: It sits, on average, just 170 meters above the sea. No Alps, no Pyrenees, nothing to hide behind. Just forest, steppe, and rivers.
And the rivers were the secret. They ran north and south, and their sources almost touched.
Where they didn't, people dragged their boats over land from one river to the next. The Russians called these portages voloks.
Whoever held the rivers held the plain. In 1300, the Principality of Moscow covered about 20,000 square kilometers.
By 1462, 430,000. By 1584, 5.4 million. Moscow grew like nothing else in Europe.
Even the Urals, the line between Europe and Asia, never stopped anyone. Their highest peak is under 1,900 meters.
In 1582, a Cossack band crossed them and took the capital of the Khanate of Sibir.
From there, Siberia was the same trick on a bigger scale. Rivers, short portages, boat after boat.
Fifty-seven years later, in 1639, Russians were standing on the shore of the Pacific.
Now look west. Europe is the opposite. Peninsula after peninsula, cut off by mountains and seas.
Iberia behind the Pyrenees, Italy behind the Alps, Scandinavia across the Baltic, Britain across the channel.
Every corner was easy to defend and hard to conquer. Russia had no walls to stop it. Europe had walls everywhere.
And a land with no walls is also a land with no safe border. The only way to feel safe was to keep going.

eventi.testo: No walls meant no safe border

scene.testo: But a plain with no walls cuts both ways. In 1237, the Mongols rode in. Within three years, they had burned the cities of the Rus.
Kiev, the greatest of them, fell in 1240. For the next two centuries, the Rus princes paid tribute to the Golden Horde.
And one small town got very good at it, Moscow. Its prince Ivan, nicknamed Kalita, the money bag, collected the Khan's tribute.

eventi.descrizione: 14th-century Moscow prince, fur hat, holding a money bag

scene.testo: The Khan trusted him and the other princes had to pay him. Moscow learned how a steppe empire runs a huge flat land.
One ruler, one tax, messengers riding in relays across the plain. It also learned to swallow its rivals.
Novgorod was a rich merchant republic in the north, run by a town assembly that rang a bell to call its citizens.
In 1478, Moscow took the city, abolished the assembly, and carried the bell back to Moscow.
In 1480, a Mongol army and a Russian army faced each other across the Ugra River. Neither attacked.
The Horde turned back and Moscow simply took its place.
Here's the strange part. The same Mongols also conquered China. The two places that became giants had the same teacher.
Europe? In 1241, the Mongols crushed armies in Poland and Hungary. Then, in 1242, they turned around.
Europe never got a conqueror big enough to force it together. Before we follow the crown, an honest ask: subscribing really helps. Thank you.
In 1453, Constantinople fell to the Ottomans and Moscow became the strongest Orthodox Christian power left.
Its monks had a slogan for it. Two Romes have fallen, the third stands, and there will be no fourth.
Moscow had already married into the old empire. In 1472, Ivan III wed the niece of the last Byzantine emperor.

eventi.descrizione: 15th-century Russian grand prince, long beard, fur robe

scene.testo: He took Byzantium's double-headed eagle as Russia's emblem. In 1547, Ivan IV was crowned not just prince, but Tsar, from Caesar.

eventi.descrizione: 16th-century first Tsar of Russia, crown, dark robe

scene.testo: And in Russia, the church stood behind the throne, not against it. In 1721, Peter the Great abolished the patriarch.

eventi.descrizione: Russian emperor, tall, wig, dark coat

eventi.testo: Church placed under a government office

scene.testo: In Europe, power was split from the start. In 1077, an emperor stood in the snow at Canossa for three days, begging the Pope.
In 1517, the Reformation split the church itself. And the Thirty Years War that followed killed millions.

eventi.testo: The Thirty Years War killed millions

scene.testo: It ended in 1648 with the Peace of Westphalia. That's our 1648. The same year a Russian sailor reached the end of Asia, Europe signed a peace that left it in pieces.
But what really pulled Russia east wasn't kings or priests, it was fur. Siberian furs were so valuable they were called soft gold.

eventi.testo: Siberian furs were called soft gold

scene.testo: The Stroganovs, a family of merchants, had hired that Cossack band in 1582 to push their fur business east.
The peoples of Siberia were forced to pay tribute in furs called yasak. Every few hundred kilometers, the Cossacks built a wooden fort.
Tomsk in 1604, Yeniseysk in 1619, Yakutsk in 1632. Fort after fort, all the way east.
In the middle of the 1600s, Siberian furs brought the Tsar more than 100,000 rubles a year, up to a tenth of all state income.

eventi.testo: Furs funded a tenth of the state

scene.testo: And sable doesn't come back fast. When the hunters had cleared one region, they moved on to the next and the next.
Between the 1620s and the 1690s, the tribute furs coming out of western Siberia fell by about 45 percent.
The hunt went all the way to the Pacific and then across it to Alaska, which Russia sold to the United States in 1867 for 7.2 million dollars.
Russia's expansion was, at its heart, a business, and it worked. But the same flat land would do something else.
Europe had its would-be unifiers. Rome got stuck at the Rhine after losing three legions in the German forests in 9 AD.
Charlemagne built an empire, and his grandson split it in three in 843.

eventi.descrizione: Frankish emperor, crown, long mustache, royal cloak

scene.testo: In 1709, Sweden's king marched into Russia and lost his army at Poltava.
Napoleon came closest. By 1812, he dominated most of the continent. Then he marched into Russia with more than half a million men.

eventi.descrizione: French emperor, bicorne hat, blue military coat

scene.testo: He even took Moscow in September 1812, and found it empty. Then the city burned, more than two thirds of it.
The plain gave him no walls to break, just distance. The Russians fell back, burned what they left behind, and let winter do the rest.
By the time what was left of his army crossed the Berezina River, only about 27,000 men were still fit to fight.
In 1941, Hitler tried again with more than three million troops. Same plain, same distance, same winter.
By December, his soldiers could see Moscow's spires, and that was as far as they got.
The land that let Russia grow without walls is the same land that swallowed the two men who came closest to uniting Europe by force.
So Russia won the land, but who won the money? Today, the average person in the European Union produces about 43,000 dollars a year.
The average Russian, about 15,000, almost three times less.
Historians like Joel Mokyr and Walter Scheidel think Europe's broken map is part of the reason.

eventi.descrizione: Economic historian, glasses, grey hair, academic jacket
Stanford historian, glasses, dark hair, blazer

scene.testo: In a Europe of many states, if one king crushed your business or banned your book, you crossed a border.

eventi.testo: Cross a border, escape the ruler

scene.testo: Rulers had to compete for merchants, scientists, and ideas, or lose them to the neighbors.
When Portugal turned down Columbus, he crossed the border and kept asking until Spain said yes.

eventi.descrizione: 15th-century Genoese navigator, long hair, red cap, dark cloak

scene.testo: When the Inquisition banned Galileo's books, his last one was printed in the Dutch Republic in 1638.

eventi.descrizione: Italian astronomer, long white beard, dark scholar robe

scene.testo: In Russia, there was nowhere to go. One ruler, one church, and peasants tied to the land.
Russia only abolished serfdom in 1861, and most of that land is nearly empty. Siberia is 77 percent of Russia, but home to about a quarter of its people.
Is that destiny? No. Russia's economy has grown fast before, and not every European country is rich.
But here's the final twist. Even Russia's plain couldn't hold everything together. In 1991, the Soviet Union split into 15 countries.
Russia lost about a quarter of its territory and about half its people.
So let's score it. Geography: Russia got a plain with no walls. Europe got peninsulas and mountains.
Resources: Russia got fur and endless land. Europe got ports and trade. History: Russia had the Mongols and one Tsar.
Europe had a Pope against an Emperor. Decisions: Russia chose one ruler. Europe, in the end, chose to compete.
The plain gave Russia its size. The walls gave Europe its rivals, and the rivals made it rich.
And Europe did finally come together. Not with an army, but with treaties. Today, 27 countries share one market.
Think back to 1648. A Russian sailor at the edge of Asia, diplomats in Westphalia. One side was building the biggest country on Earth. The other agreed to stay in pieces.

eventi.testo: One built a giant, one stayed split

scene.testo: Russia won the land. Europe won the money.
